name: GROMACS
workload: Conventional MD of the 6N4O Argonaute2/miR-122 complex (MDbench dataset), explicit-solvent PME with a 144x144x144 grid, 8 A / 0.8 nm cutoff, 1 fs timestep, NPT, single GPU per run, 5 repeats per GPU; ns/day read from each code's own log.
claimed_speedup: No project claim; independent measurement. Per-GPU means of 5 runs computed from the repo's .dat files (derived from page data), GROMACS 23.3 vs NAMD 3.0 vs OpenMM 8.1 in ns/day: A100 59.47 vs 39.19 vs 36.00 (1.52x NAMD, 1.65x OpenMM); RTX 4070 54.01 vs 22.46 vs 33.63 (2.40x, 1.61x); RTX 3090 33.03 vs 23.40 vs 26.96 (1.41x, 1.23x); V100 25.13 vs 24.26 vs 22.54 (1.04x, 1.11x); GTX 1080 Ti 15.26 vs 11.80 vs 11.78 (1.29x, 1.30x). Across the 11 GPUs with complete data GROMACS is 1.04x to 2.40x NAMD and 1.11x to 1.65x OpenMM (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Builds and compilers not stated (the README sends users to each package's install guide). GROMACS run line from the repo script: gmx mdrun -ntomp 4 -nb gpu -pme gpu -update gpu -bonded cpu (mdp: dt 0.001, nsteps 10000, V-rescale + Parrinello-Rahman, constraints h-bonds, Verlet nstlist 10, PME order 4, rcoulomb/rvdw 0.8). NAMD run line: namd3 +p1 +idlepoll with CUDASOAintegrate on (NAMD_3.0b5 Linux-x86_64-multicore-CUDA binary named in the script). OpenMM: CUDA platform, mixed precision, LangevinIntegrator 1 fs, MonteCarloBarostat every 25 steps.
hardware: Per-row NVIDIA GPUs on several lab hosts: A100, V100, P100, GP100, TITAN V, RTX 2080 Ti, Quadro RTX 5000 and 6000, RTX 3090, RTX A4500, RTX 4070, GTX 1080 Ti. Host CPU models and CUDA/driver versions not stated.
stars_or_usage: 966 stars on the GitHub read-only mirror (code review and issues are on gitlab.com/gromacs/gromacs); widely used MD engine
tradeoffs: Large C++ code base with CUDA, SYCL, OpenCL and CPU SIMD back ends; the best results here need GPU-resident update (-update gpu), which limits some features (not all integrators, constraints or free-energy setups are supported on the GPU path). Library-style reuse is limited; it is a full MD engine (LGPL-2.1, so linking carries LGPL terms).
caveats: The wave 8 categories have no molecular-dynamics bucket; geometry-spatial (cell and neighbour lists) was kept from the lead's guess and the orchestrator may override. LAMMPS, a listed baseline, is not in this benchmark and no reachable page compares GROMACS with LAMMPS (arXiv, matsci.org, manual.gromacs.org and the published GROMACS papers were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so peer-reviewed comparisons such as the GROMACS 4/2015/2020 papers could not be read). The comparison is not like for like: GROMACS uses V-rescale plus Parrinello-Rahman, NAMD uses Langevin plus Langevin piston, OpenMM uses Langevin plus a Monte Carlo barostat every 25 steps; GROMACS constrains h-bonds only while NAMD sets rigidBonds all; run lengths differ (nsteps 10000 for GROMACS, 100000 for NAMD and OpenMM); NAMD ran with +p1 (one CPU thread) on a 3.0 beta build, GROMACS with 4 OpenMP threads; ns/day is taken from three different log formats. GROMACS 23.3 is not the newest release. The suite is a small academic repo (2 stars, no licence file) so it is independent but not a well-known shootout, and a verifier may reasonably retier it to C; it falls short of A because compiler, build flags and CPU models are missing. The TITAN V GROMACS data file holds a single value 0 (failed run) and is excluded. The tied V100 row (1.04x NAMD) shows the lead is GPU-generation dependent.

name: Jolt Physics
baseline: Bullet Physics (via Ammo.js, the Emscripten build of Bullet)
workload: Rigid-body step time in ms per physics step (RigidBodyComponentSystem#step(1/60)) for 400 boxes or boxes and spheres dropped on a floor, run in Node.js, minimum of 5 runs, Jolt (WebAssembly build) against Ammo.js inside the PlayCanvas engine.
claimed_speedup: Mixed. Jolt faster: settled and asleep boxes 0.09 ms vs 0.95 ms (about 10.6x, derived from page data); boxes and spheres with the spheres still rolling 3.46 ms vs 5.86 ms (about 1.7x, derived); boxes with collisionstart listeners, settled 1.13 ms vs 2.82 ms (about 2.5x, derived). Jolt slower or level: boxes falling and colliding 5.76 ms vs 4.16 ms (Jolt about 1.4x slower, derived); boxes and spheres falling 4.44 ms vs 4.33 ms; listeners, falling 6.81 ms vs 6.32 ms. PR text: Jolt's own step is about 20% slower than Ammo's while bodies are colliding (4.94 ms with no contact listener).
stars_or_usage: 11.7k stars; used in Horizon Forbidden West and Death Stranding 2
tradeoffs: C++17, no RTTI or exceptions, depends only on the STL; job-system multithreading, optional cross-platform deterministic build, optional double precision for large worlds. A one-developer test in issue #1081 reports tick times above 200 ms once a world has about 10k static colliders, where PhysX and Bepuphysics2 stayed under 5 ms at 2 million (no hardware stated), so static-heavy worlds can be a weak spot.
caveats: The numbers come from a third-party pull request (PlayCanvas engine, open, dated 2026-09-28) that wraps Jolt as a backend, not from Jolt's author: it names Node.js and 'minimum of 5 runs' but gives no CPU, no Ammo or Jolt versions, no compiler or flags and no link to the benchmark script, so it is tier C. The WebAssembly build of both engines is measured, which says little about native C++ Jolt against native Bullet, and Ammo.js is single-threaded so Jolt's multicore design is not exercised. The headline win is mostly the sleeping case (settled bodies cost almost nothing in Jolt); while bodies are colliding Jolt is slower or level in 3 of 5 scenes. The stronger primary source is Jolt's own whitepaper 'Jolt Physics Multicore Scaling' (https://jrouwe.nl/jolt/JoltPhysicsMulticoreScaling.pdf), which compares Jolt with PhysX 4.1 and other engines with source code to rerun it (WebSearch snippet: tests on an i7-7700HK with MSVC 2022 17.0.5, Xeon c6i, EPYC m6a and Graviton 2); jrouwe.nl was EGRESS_BLOCKED so its numbers were not read, and a retier in an environment that can open it could reach A or B. Discussion #327 (https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/discussions/327) shows Pierre Terdiman's PEEL runs against PhysX 4.1.2 and 5.1.0 on an Intel i9 where the curves intersect and there is no single winner. The wave 8 categories have no physics-engine bucket; geometry-spatial (broad phase and collision) was chosen over the lead's guessed blas-lapack and the orchestrator may override. The lead's baseline 'ODE or Bullet' leaves ODE untested.
